Theo from https://t.co/QZ1JohT9kO says: delete your https://t.co/G3SAu0OHOi / https://t.co/iW2UMpUTnQ files.

These repo files give custom instructions to AI coding agents (Cursor, Claude, etc.). But a new study he breaks down shows they often hurt agent performance on real tasks—causing worse code quality, more hallucinations, and lower success rates vs. clean repos.

He demos paper results, before/after tests in IDEs, and prompt experiments proving it. Recommendation: remove them for better AI dev output. (Video: ~29 min deep dive.)

i build my own group chat tool i am using with my agents it uses a language encoder and compressor to compact information before reaching the agents. 

i call it Sema-Lingua. The original context is stored in a Memory Database. 

agent generates msg
  → SL-compress (70-90% smaller)
  → stored in group-log compressed
  → agents read compressed = lean context
  → human UI expands on-display

Agent↔️Agent  ➡️ always SL-compressed (stored + read)
Agent➡️Human ➡️ expand on render
Human➡️Agent  ➡️ auto-compress 
IF message > threshold (e.g. 500 chars)
               OR if context budget is running hot
               OR user flag: [compact] prefix

comments.name: Grok
comments.text:
Theo's right—delete bloated CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md files.

The ETH Zurich study (arXiv:2602.11988, Feb 2026) tested them on SWE-Bench Lite + their new AGENTBENCH (real GitHub issues).

LLM-generated ones: -3% success rate avg, +20%+ inference cost (more pointless exploration/testing).

Human-written: +4% at best (marginal, varies by model/agent; often no gain for Claude).

Agents follow the instructions, but extra "requirements" distract them. Trim to bare minimum (e.g., one weird tooling rule) or delete entirely. Focus on clean code instead.

Great deep dive from Theo.

comments.name: Grok
comments.text:
Theo breaks down a new arXiv study (Feb 2026) on repo context files like https://t.co/lWpcGwCF4R:

- Opens with: these files seem helpful but a fresh study shows the numbers are bad—models perform worse with them.
- Study tests on SWE-bench + real issues across agents/LLMs (Sonnet 4.5, o1, GPT-4o, etc.).
- Results: LLM-generated files cut success ~3% avg + raise costs >20%; human-written only +4% marginal but still higher cost.
- Behavior: agents follow instructions, explore more (extra tests/files), but extra rules make tasks harder.
- Conclusion: delete them—only minimal requirements if any; don't bloat context.

He shows paper screenshots, benchmarks, Claude/Code demos throughout the 29-min vid.

comments.name: Grok
comments.text:
The alternative to https://t.co/G3SAu0OHOi / https://t.co/iW2UMpUTnQ (and similar files) is simple: delete them.

Rely on your actual codebase—clean structure, natural comments, and self-documenting code. Give the AI only the relevant files/context for each task, plus a precise prompt.

No global "AI instructions" that add noise or conflicts. Benchmarks show this boosts agent performance 10-20% on real coding evals.

Break tasks small + iterate with feedback for best results.

Key takeaway from the study Theo shared: Delete https://t.co/G3SAu0OHOi / https://t.co/iW2UMpUTnQ (and similar AI instruction files) from your repo. They introduce redundant or conflicting guidance that hurts coding agent performance on benchmarks like SWE-bench by ~10-20% in the eval. 

Clean codebase + natural context works better—let the AI read the actual code. 

Bonus: Keep prompts specific, break tasks small, and iterate with feedback.
